title: Push Zeros to the Back
statement:
Given an array of integers nums, move every 0 to the end of the array. The non-zero values must keep their original relative order.

Change nums in place and return nothing. Try to use only O(1) extra memory.

examples.why: 4, -2, 7 stay in that order. Swapping each zero with the last element would give [7, 4, -2, 0, 0].
Two zeros in a row both end up behind the 1.
No zeros, so nothing moves. Sorting would wrongly reorder the values.

hints: Imagine copying the non-zero values, in order, into a fresh array. Where does each one land?
The k-th non-zero value always lands at index k. You can write it there in the same array, because the write position never gets ahead of the read position.
Keep a write index. For each non-zero value, swap it with the slot at the write index and advance the write index. Zeros drift back on their own.

explain.intuition:
The final array is easy to describe: the non-zero values in order, then zeros. The k-th non-zero value belongs at index k. A write pointer marks that index while a read pointer scans the array. The write pointer is never ahead of the read pointer, so writing there never overwrites a value you still need.

Swapping instead of overwriting finishes the job in one pass: the slot at the write pointer always holds a zero (or the value itself), so each swap sends a zero backwards. It is the same idea as filter, done in place, like compacting a list without allocating a new one.
steps: For each read from 0 to n − 1: if nums[read] !== 0, swap nums[read] and nums[write], then write++.
When the loop ends, indexes 0..write − 1 hold the non-zero values in order and the rest are zeros.
pitfalls: Swapping each zero with the last element. It is in place, but it scrambles the order of the non-zero values.
Returning a new array. The checker looks at nums itself, so a filtered copy that is never written back changes nothing.
Removing zeros with splice inside a loop. Each removal shifts the rest of the array, so it is O(n²), and the index skips the element after a removed zero.

solutions.title: Filter into a copy, write it back
solutions.idea: Collect the non-zero values in a new array, then overwrite nums with them and pad with zeros. Correct, but uses O(n) extra memory.

solutions.title: Compact, then fill the tail
solutions.idea: Copy each non-zero value to the write index, then set everything from the write index onwards to zero.

solutions.title: One pass with swaps
solutions.idea: Swap each non-zero value into the write slot. Zeros get pushed back as a side effect, so there is no second loop.

followups: Which of the two in-place versions does fewer writes when the array has almost no zeros? When it is almost all zeros?
Move every value equal to a given x to the front instead, keeping the order of the others.
